A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ViBES research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete supplementary sections are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original ViBES results for conversational behavior, speech, talking-head synthesis and gesture generation in Tables 2–5, plus qualitative results in the supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 reports original ViBES results, including the revised conversational evaluation and recomputed talking-head comparisons, alongside retained speech, gesture and qualitative results.

M1.justification: The modality experts, attention routing, tokenization procedure and fractional RoPE remain unchanged. The body-token rate changes from 7.25 to 6.25 fps, correcting consistency with the retained 25-fps clock and fourfold downsampling rather than establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: Section 5.2 changes the stated quantitative talking-head test data from the YouTube split of Converse3D to TFHP. TFHP already appeared in v1's training and qualitative evaluations, so this is a limited reported coverage revision. Other tasks and corpus sources remain; Seamless Interaction is added only to the descriptive dataset comparison.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same comparison methods. Table 2 still evaluates SynTalker, EMAGE, LoM, T2M, MotionGPT and MoMask; the talking-head, speech and gesture comparator sets also remain unchanged. The added ground-truth row supplies a reference.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 replaces GPT-4o behavior ratings with a Q2M retrieval protocol on 4,921 samples, specifying balanced 16-plus-16 batches, strict action matching, relaxed conversational matching, and retrieval/distribution metrics. Section 5.2 adopts ARTalk's evaluation implementation and reports recomputing baseline checkpoints. TFHP-only model training was already documented in v1, so that restriction is retained rather than newly introduced.

E4.justification: The attention-ablation observation and qualitative case studies, including the Runway application and supplementary head/motion comparisons, are retained. No new controlled ablation, robustness test or error analysis appears; the replacement benchmark scores are evaluation results rather than additional diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The revised metrics do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the three behavior-rating results with retrieval and distribution results, including ViBES R1-Balanced 0.467 and FID 93.9. Table 4 changes every method's scores: ViBES LVE/MOD/FDD changes from 12.88/8.27/2.76 to 10.87/2.29/6.05 under revised evaluation, precluding a same-setting performance comparison. Tables 3 and 5 retain their values. Table 1 replaces the 1,000-hour corpus entry with N/A.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 introduces a modified retrieval-correctness definition: exact paired-motion matching for action queries, but any conversational gesture for conversational queries, combined through weighted precision. This changes the metric's mathematical definition. The attention and fractional-RoPE equations remain unchanged, with no added proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: a unified speech–language–behavior agent, the large conversational corpus, preserved speech competence and superior conversational/social behavior. The roughly 1,000-hour claim remains in the introduction despite the revised table and shortened conclusion.

C2.justification: The evaluation discussion shifts from instruction execution and social-appropriateness shortcomings to retrieval alignment and one-to-many gesture matching, and adds an explanation of incompatible LVE conventions. The conclusion substantially replaces its limitations: physical interaction, long-horizon memory, real-time control and backbone portability disappear, while insufficient training-data scale, underused LLM reasoning and evaluator reliability become explicit concerns.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Q2M encoder and motion representation, identifies ARTalk code/checkpoint reuse, and corrects token-rate reporting. It removes the old behavior-judge prompt and the speech-judging protocol description. Appendix 7.3 retains model sizes, four L40S GPUs, approximately one week of training and the learning rate; the code/data availability promise is unchanged.

R1.justification: Eight cited works are added, including Seamless Interaction and CLIP, while Video-Bench and VBench are removed with the former evaluation rationale. The substantive positioning against LoM, SOLAMI and existing multimodal architectures remains largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in Sections 5.1, 5.2 and the conclusion, with shortened dataset-processing passages. The former supplementary benchmark subsection is deleted and the following subsection renumbered. The overall organization and most introductory, architectural and supplementary prose remain stable.

P2.justification: Localized display changes include rebuilding Table 2 as a full-width comparison with additional columns, adding a Table 1 row and caption qualification, and reordering Table 4 metrics. Figure 2 is resized, Figure 4 relocates, and the obsolete Figure 12 evaluation prompt is removed. The other figures retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: Using a common ARTalk implementation improves the comparability of Table 4, and the new conversational protocol specifies its sample composition and matching rules. However, it replaces direct social-appropriateness assessment with retrieval that accepts any conversational gesture, while retaining broad social-competence claims. Protocol details for the unchanged speech scores also disappear. These gains and losses leave the net effect on evidential quality uncertain.
